# Assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at sites within Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area

```{r load packages, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

## Project Summary:

*Once you have completed this entire assignment, come back and write a project summary here that covers the aims, research questions, and basic methods of this study.*

This study aims to explore the differences in owl limpet populations across different beaches in Southern California. We aim to answer the question: Are there significant differences in limpet sizes (shell length and mass), territory sizes, and density of limpets in each transect across the sampled beaches within the sample years? Over the course of several years, the MCRS program recorded data on limpets from Treasure Cove, Shaws Cove, Heisler Park, and Coronal del Mar, all locations in Newport Beach and northern Laguna Beach. Limpet shell length was measured in mm using calipers, and limpet territory was measured by counting squares on a mesh net with known square area. Mass of limpets was calculated from shell length, using conversation rates pulled from outside data. Density of limpets per territory is calculated using the sample size and area of each territory.

To explore the relationships between these variables, we used R to create visualizations of the data (scatter plots, box plots, column graphs, and histograms. We then ran statistical analyses on the data, to determine the significance of the relationships between the variables at different sites. We used such tests as student's t-test, Shapiro Wilk's test, and ANOVA. We also created linear models for the relationships between variables.

You have been given data from several locations and survey years:

- 2022: Corona del Mar (CDM) - size data only, taken haphazardly

- 2023: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

- 2024: Heisler Park and Shaws Cove - size data in variable length transects, territories

- 2025: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |> #creates new data set, LimpetDensity, from NoCDMSizes
  select(transect_length_m, site, transect_num, year) |> #selects which columns to use
  group_by(transect_length_m, site, transect_num, year) |> #doing this maintains the separation in year for the Treasure Cove Surveys 
  summarize(count=n()) |> #Tells us the count in each transect
  mutate(density = count/(transect_length_m*2))#creates a new column that tells us the density of limpets in each transect
  



#limpetdensity is the column with values for limpet density in each transect
#Limpet_Density is the data set that contains the column limpetdensity 
Limpet_Density
#shows us the new data we just created 
```

#### 2.2. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}
#finding mean density across all sites 
Limpet_Density$density |> 
  mean()
#finding the standard deviation of the density across all sites
sd(Limpet_Density$density)

#finding standard error
sd(Limpet_Density$density)/sqrt(nrow(Limpet_Density))
```

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# use summarize() to calculate the mean and standard error (sd/sqrt(n)) for the two locations

LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |> #new data set to hold results of population summary
  group_by(site, year) |> #grouping data in Limpet_Density by site and year to keep data from each site seperate (and data from Treasure Cove seperate by years)
  summarise(mean_density = mean(density, na.rm = TRUE), #creates column for mean of density
            sd_density = sd(density, na.rm = TRUE), #creates column for standard deviation of density
            n = n(), #tells us how many values (and therefore transects) are in each site
            se_density = sd_density/sqrt(n)) |> #creates column for standard error of density 
  mutate_at(vars(mean_density, sd_density, se_density),
            .funs = round,1) #rounds each column to one decimal place
      
            
            
            
  
 
# Display your summary nicely using kable(). 
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)

```

#### 2.6. Does average number of owl limpets per square meter differ significantly between Heisler Park and Shaws Cove?

Filter the data to only include those sites before putting it into the `t.test()` function. These are a good comparison because they were measured in the same year with the same survey methods.

```{r t-test}
# run a t-test on your count data from each site (Limpet_Density)
ShawsHeislerDensity <- Limpet_Density |> #creating data set ShawsHeislerDensity using Limpet_Density
  filter(site == "Heisler Park" | site == "Shaws Cove") #using only values from sites Heisler Park and Shaws Cove


t.test(density ~ site   , data = ShawsHeislerDensity) #run a t-test on the relationship between density and site from the data we just created. 

```

Explain the results of this t-test. Are you surprised by this result, given the figure you made above? Why do you think the results are what they are?

Becuase the P value is greater than 0.05, we cannot reject the null hypothesis (Null hypothesis = there is no statistical difference between the density by site in Heisler Park and Shaws Cove). This makes, given that the box plot for Heisler Park looks very similar to that for Shaws Cove (similar spread, similar mean)

#### 2.8 EXTRA CREDIT: Do an ANOVA comparing Shaws, Heisler, and Treasure Cove 2025 density data (exclude 2023 so that the sample size is similar between all three). Use a Tukey post-hoc test. Explain the results.

```{r}
#oneway.test
#bartlett.test

#Exclude any years other than 2025 from the data set 
anova_density_data<-Limpet_Density |> 
  filter(year == "2025" |year == "2024")
#create a linear model for the density~site relationship
Limpet_Density_model<-lm(density~site, data = anova_density_data )

#visualize the data by creating a box plot
ggplot(anova_density_data)+
  aes(x = site, y = density)+
  geom_boxplot()

#Plot Q-Q Residuals for limpet density ~ site
plot(Limpet_Density_model, which = 2)

#run a Shapiro-Wilk normality test for the Limpet Density Model
shapiro.test(Limpet_Density_model$residuals)

#run a Bartlett test for the original data, to see if the variance is equal among treatments 
bartlett.test(density~site, data=anova_density_data)


#run anova on the limpet density model
anova(Limpet_Density_model)

#run Tukey test on the density data 
TukeyHSD(aov(density~site, data = anova_density_data))




```

Results:

Q-Q Residuals: this shows us how the actual residuals line up with the theoretical residuals in a normal distribution. Looking at this graph, we can see that they line up with the theoretical line fairly well, meaning they follow a fairly normal distribution.

Shapiro test: p-value of 0.03789 which means that the model residuals are different than normal. However, the sample size for this is relatively large, so the Shapiro test might not be accurate. Given that the Q-Q plot looked like the residuals had relatively normal distribution, we will move forward with the ANOVA.

Bartlett test of HOV: p-value of 0.02738 This means there is not homogeneity of variance. Typically this would mean not moving forward with an anova, but given that the question is asking for an ANOVA, we will run the ANOVA anyway with the understanding that there was not HOV.

Anova test: This returns with a table of values that are part of our analysis of variance for the difference sites. I don't 100% understand what all of the values that it gives us are for, but we do get a Pr value with two \*\*, telling use that there is moderately high significance with the results.

Tukey test: for the Tukey test, we get that the only two sites that were significantly different from each other, in terms of limpet density, were Treasure Cove and Shaws Cove. This was the only site pairing that had a p value of less than 0.05.

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
## Test for Homogeneity of Variance with an F-Test

# create the appropriate filter to include only Treasure Cove and CDM data
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> #create data set for just TC and CDM 
  filter(site == "Corona del Mar" | site == "Treasure Cove") #filters so only values from TC and CDM are included

  
# set the linear model for testing the assumptions
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes) #create model, run linear model on relationship between shell length and site using CDM and TC data

# Examine plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values
plot(model, which = 1) #plot the model, show plot type 1 which is the one for residuals v. fitted 

# F-test for homogeneity of variance - if p-value < 0.05 then variances are different. 
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes) #run f test for relationship between shell length and site, using the CDM TC data

# NOTE: if your sample fails this test, have no fear! Welch's t-test (the default that R uses) is okay to use with unequal variances. 

```

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?
  - No, the distribution of residuals has data clumping at either end, rather than an even distribution around the fitted line.

?shapiro.test

```{r}
## Test for normality

# examine a QQ-plot
plot(model, which = 2) #plot the model we made in the last chunk, see plot type 2, which is the QQ plot

# conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals
shapiro.test(model$residuals) #run a shapiro Wilk test on the model, specifically on the residuals of the model

```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
t.test(CDM_TC_Sizes$shell_length_mm ) #run t test on shell length column from CDM TC data
#the p-value is telling us if the shell length betweens sites are different enough to be statistically significant. 
```

#### [3.3 Graph your results using a column plot with error bars for standard error]{.underline}

For full credit, have well centered error bars and professionally labeled axes (they should not say "mean", they should say the variable name).

```{r}

  CDM_TC_Sizes |> #use CDM TC data
  group_by(site) |> #group data by site
  summarize(mean_shell= mean(shell_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE), #Create summary stats for mean of shell length, remove any NA values
            sd_shell=sd(shell_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE), #gives standard deviation of shell length, remove NA values
            n=n(), #counts how many values there are (i.e. sample size)

  ggplot( #create plot

  )+

  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mean_shell-sd_shell, #create error bars, assign min and max y values
                    ymax=mean_shell+sd_shell),
                    position = position_dodge(0.8), #tells R where to position errorbars
                    width=0.2)+ #makes error bars less wide

```

#### [3.4 - Interpret and explain the results of your test]{.underline}

Are we pretty confident that these samples were drawn from different populations? Why is the standard error so small?

We are confident that these are from different populations. The t-test returned a really small p value (2.2\^-16), so we can confidently reject the null hypothesis. (null hypothesis was that the samples were not statistically significant.)

Standard error is small because of how large our sample size is. Standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of sample size- because of the large sample size we divided sd by a fairly large number, giving us a small se.

```{r}
#graph results with column plot and se bars 
HP_SC_Sizes |> #use HP SC Size data 
  group_by(site) |> #seperate by site
  summarize(mean_shell= mean(shell_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE), #create summary values for shell length, this line does mean, then the next ones do standard deviation, sample size, and standard error.
            sd_shell=sd(shell_length_mm, na.rm=TRUE),
            n=n(),
            se_shell= sd_shell/sqrt(n)) |> 
  ggplot( #create a plot
    aes(x=site, y= mean_shell) #assign axes
  )+
  geom_col()+ #plot is a column plot (i.e. bar)
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mean_shell-sd_shell, #create error bars, assign min and max of error bars
                    ymax=mean_shell+sd_shell),
                position = position_dodge(0.8), #positions the error bars
                width=0.2)+ #assigns less wide width to error bars
  labs(title= "Shell Length at Heisler Park and Shaws Cove",
       x = "Site",
       y= "Shell Length (mm)") #label the plot with title and axes titles

```

Results:

Q-Q shows mostly normal residuals, although they do start deviating away from the theoretical line of fit at the ends of the point cluster.

Residuals v Fitted Values: This graph shows really weird clumping, lowkey not sure if I did it wrong or not. however, given that the QQ values showed slight abnormality and the Shapiro test has a really small p value, the Residuals being off from fitted values makes sense.

Shapiro test: p value is REALLY small, so residuals are different from normal.

So, from the 3 above we see that the statistical significance of the difference between Heisler and Shaws is questionable. This makes sense, given that in the graph for shell length by site, Shaws Coves mean and error bars all fit within the mean and error bar for Heisler Park.

```{r}
All_Territories_area_mass <- All_Territories |> #create new data set for territory area and limpet mass

  mutate(mass_g = 0.00009*size_mm ^ 3.0471) #computes the mass from limpet shell length
```

#### 4.6. What important assumptions of tests of linear regression do these scatter plots fail? How can you tell?

These scatter plots do not show a linear relationship between the variables, but appear to be more of an exponential relationship. As such, there is (presumably) uneven variance of distance between the mean for each data point.

```{r}

# write a linear model for the relationship, then use the plot() function on the model object to show the residuals vs. fitted values and QQ plots to assess your regression. 

linear_model <- lm(mass_g ~ territory_area_mm, All_Territories_area_mass)
#writes linear model for mass_g (x value) and territroy_area_mm (y value) relationship 

plot(linear_model)
#plots the linear model
```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?

This plot looks more like a cloud shape, so it is closer to what we assume a scatter plot representing a linear relationship should look like.

```{r scatterplot with regression line}
# plot a scatterplot log area on y axis by log mass_g on x axis, best fit regression line but no SE interval

All_Territories_area_mass |> ggplot() + #make a plot using All Territories area mass data
  aes(x=log(mass_g), y=log(territory_area_mm))+ #makes x and y axes the log of mass and territory
  geom_point()+ #point plot
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) #line of best fit, no se zone

```

```{r}
# write the linear model object and examine the residual and QQ plots
log_model <- lm(log(mass_g)~log(territory_area_mm), All_Territories_area_mass) #write a linear model of the relationship between log of mass and log of territory area in All Territories area mass data
  
plot(log_model, which = 1) #residuals v fitted plot of log model
plot(log_model, which = 2) #QQ plot of log model 
```

#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}

lm_All_Territories <- #create data for linear model of all territories data
  lm(log(territory_area_mm)~log(mass_g), #run linear model of relationship between logs of territroy and mass 
     data = All_Territories_area_mass) #use this data

lm_All_Territories #take a look at it 
summary(lm_All_Territories) #summarize it

slope<- coef(lm_All_Territories)[2] #create object "slope", tell it how to find slope
slope #look at slope

int <- coef(lm_All_Territories)[1]  #create obj. #int for intercept, tell R how to find int
int #print int value
```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903X + 8.2116**

```{r}
FenbergTerr #take a look at FenbergTerr data
```

FenbergTerr Line of best fit equation:

Y=0.8916202X+7.90973

Explain your findings!

The line of best fit equation for the Fenberg data is similar to the line of best fit equation from the All Sites Data. When you round the slope to two decimals points, they each have the same slope (0.89). Their intercepts are also similar, with a difference of only \~ 0.3. This shows that the relationship between limpet mass and territory size is very similar between the two data sets.
